_meta.description: WHAT THE OFFICE CAN ACTUALLY DO, and which code path supplies it. One row per capability, naming the means as a resolvable reference (a file and a symbol, or a lane in config/model-routing.json) and naming the verifier that exercises it. Read by workers/capability-audit.js; run by scripts/capability-audit.mjs. The narrative companion is back-office-AI-agents/docs/CAPABILITY-TOOLBOX.md, which is generated from an audit run rather than written from memory.
_meta.the_question_this_answers: The Workflow's census (workers/meeting-decisions.js) asks WHO HAS NOT PRODUCED ANYTHING. This asks the other half — DOES EACH AGENT HAVE THE MEANS ITS ROLE REQUIRES — and the two catch different failures. A census sees a role that STOPPED working. It cannot see a role that NEVER STARTED, because an agent that was never dispatched anything is not idle, it is absent from the question. That is exactly how The Designer existed for two months with a documented capability and no code path behind it.

verdicts.SUPPLIED: The named means resolves — the file exists and exports the symbol, or the lane exists and is routable — AND a verifier exercises it.
verdicts.UNPROVEN: The means resolves but NOTHING exercises it. Agent 13's own standard, lifted from board task OB-001: 'A gate with no verifier exercising it is UNPROVEN, never CALLED.' Applied to a capability rather than a gate.
verdicts.UNSUPPLIED: No code path supplies it. Either the manifest says so outright (`supplied_by.kind: "none"`) or the named reference does not resolve. THIS IS THE DESIGNER'S OLD STATE and the verdict this whole file exists to surface.

_meta.how_to_extend: A NON-EXHAUSTIVE starting list, to be extended rather than treated as the scope — the same wording OB-001 carries, for the same reason. Adding a capability to the office means adding a row here IN THE SAME SESSION, under the spec-tables maintenance rule. A capability with no row is invisible to the audit, and an audit that reports 'no gaps' because nobody told it about a capability is worse than no audit.
_meta.what_this_is_not: NOT a skills library. campus/brain-export/skills/ holds techniques another project could import; this is an inventory of what THIS office can do with THIS wiring. Conflating them is how a skills library fills up with documentation of local plumbing.
_meta.bible_quotes_are_verbatim: Every `bible_claim` is quoted from back-office-AI-agents/AGENTS-CHARACTER-CORE-v2.md, not paraphrased. A paraphrase of a role is where an invented capability gets in: it reads as the bible's claim one session later, and then the audit is measuring the manifest against itself.

answer-quality-scoring.what: Score an answer 0-1. A LENGTH PROXY, not a quality judgment: min(1, characters / 800). No model reads the question or the answer.

supplied_by.caveat: READ THIS BEFORE TRUSTING ANY QUALITY NUMBER IN THIS OFFICE. UPDATED 2026-08-16 (second session). The verdict stays SUPPLIED because the code path resolves and is exercised — but what it supplies is a measure of ANSWER LENGTH, and twelve consumers treat it as a quality judgment: the mood engine, the follow-up band, capability-gap detection, each persona's escalation_threshold, the Hebrew gap note, the journal line, reports.quality, the client-facing fact pack's AVG(quality), the meeting agenda, the improvement-loop stats trigger, and the Lead QA's cross-embodiment comparison. OB-080 IS NOW CLOSED: there was a SECOND formula (an inline /600 in _askNotebookX() against this one's /800, so the same answer scored 33% higher on notebook-x) and the two are UNIFIED AT 800 from 2026-08-16T00:00:00Z. 800 survived because it was the declared formula while /600 was an undeclared inline copy, and because it is the information-preserving direction: a row that saturates at 800 also saturated at 600, so the useless-1.0 set can only shrink. HISTORY IS NOT RESCORED (A15) — instead reports.scorer_id was added and buildOfficeEventRow() now REFUSES a row carrying a quality with no scorer id, because the reason two divisors survived four weeks is that the rows did not say. STILL SATURATED: 101 of 120 scored notebook-x rows sat at the 1.0 ceiling under /600, where the metric carries no information. STILL A LENGTH PROXY, and it is not the office's only scorer any more — see answer-quality-judging (OB-081), which sends one answer in eight to a real evaluator. TWO SUPERVISED CALLS ON THE LIVE JUDGMENT LANE, SAME QUESTION: a correct 397-char answer scored 0.50 here and 0.88 there; a padded, vague 991-char answer scored 1.00 here and 0.07 there. The two metrics are INVERTED on that pair. That is a two-point demonstration, not the calibration — the calibration needs n>=20 and is not accumulating until judge_sampler_enabled is turned on.

cross-embodiment-comparison.what: The Lead QA's signature instrument: compare report quality across agents AND across embodiment models — 'this persona is more consistent under that provider'.

supplied_by.caveat: BUILT 2026-08-10 (learning-loop session). UPDATED 2026-08-15 — the previous caveat recorded 58 case_answer rows / 23 reliably attributed / 'insufficient sample', which had been true and was not any more; a caveat that outlives its measurement understates a capability the same way a stale 'NO TOOL' overstates a gap. Re-run 2026-08-15 against live D1: 134 rows, 99 reliably embodiment-attributed, and it produced a REAL finding for the first time rather than 'insufficient sample'. ALSO 2026-08-15: it finally has an autonomous caller. Until then it was reachable only through /api/agents/trigger and, as far as audit finding #8 could tell, had never run in production — built, SUPPLIED, and never once executed on its own. Now the Friday 09:30 qa_instruments block (config/daily-schedule.json qa_instruments_program, workers/agent-runner.js processQaInstrumentsBlock) runs it weekly. READ THE FINDING WITH ITS OWN CAVEAT: the quality score behind every number is evaluateResponseQuality()'s documented length-based placeholder heuristic, and on the first real run the DEGRADED cloudflare-fallback scored above the primary — which is at least as likely to be a fact about the metric as about the providers. 2026-08-16 — THAT SUSPICION WAS INVESTIGATED AND CONFIRMED, AND THE INSTRUMENT NOW REFUSES THE COMPARISON. It was not merely a weak metric: the two numbers came from TWO DIFFERENT FORMULAS (divisor 800 for data-center, 600 for notebook-x), and because Claude serves only data-center while Gemini and cloudflare-fallback serve only notebook-x, provider and divisor are perfectly confounded — no sample size separates them. buildFindings() now calls scoresAreComparable() (workers/quality-metric.js) and emits `comparison_refused_confounded` in place of `embodiment_quality_gap` whenever the pooled scores come from different divisors, naming the remedy rather than qualifying a ranking (a reader takes the ranking and leaves the caveat). Verified live post-deploy against real D1: the false finding is gone and the refusal is what the instrument now reports. It STILL ranks legitimately when the compared embodiments share a project — proven by scripts/verify-quality-metric.js §4, which would catch a gate that had degraded into a blanket refusal. Every rendered number now carries METRIC_DISCLOSURE, its scoring project, and its saturation count.

answer-quality-judging.what: Evaluate an answer AGAINST THE QUESTION with a real model, on a 1-in-8 sample, so the length proxy above can be calibrated. This is the function the length proxy is not: it reads the question.

supplied_by.caveat: LIVE IN PRODUCTION since the owner turned it on 2026-08-16 00:52 Israel; the code default is still OFF — read the first clause before the second, because a documented switch state is a claim about code and production is a separate claim (KFM-21). STATE READ FROM PRODUCTION 2026-08-16: n=3 judged, 0 paced_out, 0 lane_error, 0 unparseable. correlate() returns insufficient_sample and reports nothing else, which is the instrument behaving correctly. THE PREVIOUS PROJECTION OF n=20 'around 2026-08-19' IS STRUCK, and how it was wrong is the useful part: it multiplied a declared 12.5% sampling rate the selector did NOT deliver by a daily volume ('40-130 answers') never checked against D1. Both were plausible, both were written down, and their product was published as a forecast. THE SELECTOR WAS BROKEN AND THE POOLED RATE HID IT: hashToUnit() divided FNV-1a out of its top 32 bits, which multiplication barely moves with the trailing bytes of an input — and every case id the office asks in one day shares a 15-character prefix, differing only in the last three digits. Across the full namespace it selected 12.09% (correct-looking); PER WORKING DAY it had sd 28.9 against a uniform 4.7, a median of 8 selectable of 200, and 80 of 260 days on which NOTHING was selectable at any rate. On the office's 125 real asked ids the realized rate was 2.4%, and 2026-08-13 — a full working day, 22 asks — would have selected none. Fixed 2026-08-16 with a fmix32 finalizer (KFM-29); THE RATE, THE DIVISOR AND THE METRIC ARE UNCHANGED — the fix makes the realized rate equal the declared one. Zero rows existed under the broken selector, so nothing was rescored (A15); that is timing, not design. quality_judgements.selector_id now records what selected each row, the 3 pre-deploy rows carry hash-select-v1@0.125 and are NOT part of the fixed selector's sample, and runCalibration() refuses to pool rows across selectors. REVISED PROJECTION, assumptions named so it can be falsified the way the last one was: 25.2 answers per full working day (measured over 5 days) x 0.125 = ~3.15 selections/day against a send capacity of 6/day, so THE RATE BINDS AND THE PACING CAP DOES NOT — n=20 lands around 2026-08-24 if volume holds and Friday stays light. The mechanism itself is proven: two supervised live calls on the judgment lane (Cerebras, free tier) returned parseable scores of 0.88 and 0.07 for a good and a padded answer to the same question. But a proven mechanism with a broken sampler is not a measurement, and neither is one with n=3. THE POINT IS CALIBRATION, NOT A BETTER SCORE: whether the cheap score correlates with a real one at all. correlate() REFUSES below n=20 or when the cheap scores have no spread; the likeliest outcome remains cheap_score_has_no_variance, because a metric sitting at 1.0 for 84% of answers has nothing to correlate with — and that would itself be the finding. Sampling is 1 in 8 by a deterministic hash of the case id (reproducible, so the sample can be audited); SENDING is capped by the judgment lane's 20-second unknown-cap pacing floor, not by a counter, and cases pacing turns away are recorded as paced_out rather than vanishing. KNOWN BIAS, stated: selection is position-independent — TRUE ONLY SINCE THE FIX, and it was documented as true for a month while being the opposite; sending is not position-independent, since within a block the earliest selected case takes the only slot.

answer-quality-judging.cost: none — judgment lane, Cerebras free tier. The cost objection to a real evaluation was checked and is false; the binding constraint is pacing.

growth-trend-watch.what: Measure every store that only grows — the verify suite, the report archive, per-agent journals, BOARD.md, TOKEN-BUDGET.md, the insert-only D1 tables — and report the change since the last measurement.

supplied_by.caveat: IT CAPS NOTHING AND RETIRES NOTHING, deliberately. KNOWN-FAILURE-MODES KFM-20 asks for a cap, a retirement path, OR AT MINIMUM A TREND SOMEONE READS; a cap is a policy decision that belongs to the owner and the trend is the part that was missing across seven consecutive sweeps (audit #12). It has an autonomous caller from day one — .github/workflows/weekly-capability-audit.yml — because a detection primitive with no consumer is the exact defect it was built in response to, and this project already owns one (back-office tools/repo-size-hygiene-check, whose own README records "R7 — nothing calls this"). That tool is NOT this one: it measures bytes on disk against a 2GB/4GB threshold, and none of #18/#19/#20 is a disk-space problem. COVERAGE IS PARTIAL IN CI AND SAYS SO: the weekly job holds no credential for either private repo, so back-office metrics come back not_measured WITH A REASON, never as zero, and each metric trends against the last run that measured THAT metric rather than the previous run. The CI run reports but does not extend the ledger (no commit step) — OB-085.

growth-trend-watch.cost: none — filesystem reads plus one read-only Worker trigger (growth_counts)

invocation-budget.what: Keep a per-invocation subrequest budget for a scheduled tick: reserve a guaranteed floor for client cases, size each batch to what actually fits, and record what did not fit as DEFERRED rather than dropping it.

supplied_by.caveat: THE LIMITS ARE MEASURED, NOT QUOTED (subrequest_probe trigger, live Worker, 2026-08-16): external fetch() 50 per invocation; Durable Object stub calls 200, with a DIFFERENT error string ('Too many API requests', which never appears in the incident rows); D1 and KV >=400 with no refusal, i.e. NOT the constraint. Cloudflare's own prose reads as though D1 and KV count, and the first calibration built from it throttled a tick to three cases when the platform allowed forty. THE METER IS EXACT FOR BINDINGS AND CONSERVATIVE FOR THE REST: meterEnv() wraps D1/KV/DO/AI/APP_API and meterGlobalFetch() swaps the global for the tick, so the ledger counts real spend rather than an estimate. The one row NOT measured is the APP_API service binding, charged at a full fetch because probing it spends real Anthropic budget. WHAT IT DOES NOT DO: it cannot interrupt a block mid-flight. Non-case blocks are admitted or deferred on a BLOCK_COST estimate, and those estimates are provisional - derived from a stub harness that measured a real meeting at 12 when the live tick measured 31. Every tick now records each block's real cost in its `admissions` array, so the next session can replace them with production numbers instead of scaled guesses.

invocation-budget.verifier_note: 103 checks. Sections 5-6 execute the REAL runScheduledBlock() for every tick of Sun-Thu, Friday and Saturday under counting bindings and fail if any tick exceeds either measured limit - the mechanization of KFM-31. Proven against the pre-change code, which fails 8 of 11 ticks.
invocation-budget.cost: none - pure bookkeeping. It spends no provider and makes no model call; it only decides how much of a tick's platform budget each kind of work may use.

case-engine-in-durable-object.what: Run a case batch inside a Durable Object instead of the Worker, behind a switch.

supplied_by.caveat: BUILT, DEPLOYED, AND SHIPPED OFF - and the measurement says it should STAY off, which is the finding rather than the caution. OB-074 was opened believing a Durable Object gets 'roughly 150' subrequests against the Worker's 50. MEASURED 2026-08-16: it gets 50, identical, with the identical error. Moving one batch inside one DO call relocates the same ceiling and buys nothing. What a Durable Object does give is a FRESH 50 PER INVOCATION, so real capacity would come from calling it many times (the Worker allows 200 such calls) - a fan-out design this module is not. AN EARLIER READING OF THIS PROBE SAID >=120 AND WAS WRONG: the DO route ignored its `kind` parameter and measured D1 while the label said fetch. Recorded rather than quietly corrected, because it is a wrong number that AGREED WITH THE EXPECTED ANSWER and survived a deploy. Gate: SIM_KV simulation-state.case_do_enabled, absent = OFF. The switch is the owner's to flip.

case-engine-in-durable-object.verifier_note: Section 6b proves inertness by RUNNING a real case tick with the flag absent and counting calls to the DO case route (zero), not by reading the source. Also proves absent/null/'true'-the-string all resolve to OFF, and that agent-runner registered the runner so the path is not a dead end if it is ever switched on.
case-engine-in-durable-object.cost: none in provider terms, but NOT free: when switched on it adds one Durable Object round trip per batch, which is itself a metered subrequest, in exchange for zero extra outbound headroom (measured). That is the argument for leaving it off.

_output_kind_producers_meta: WHICH CAPABILITY COULD PRODUCE EACH KIND OF OUTPUT A ROLE IS FOR. This is the join that makes the audit's load-bearing half possible: `agents.<id>.output_kinds` says what the role produces, and this says which capability would have to work for that to happen. It lives here as DATA rather than as a string match inside workers/capability-audit.js, because 'a visual_asset comes from the image lane' is a judgement about this office and not something a module should infer from a substring. A kind with an EMPTY producer list is reported as `unmapped` — a gap in this file rather than necessarily in the office — and deliberately not as a gap in the office, because the two have different fixes.

1.name: The Perfectionist
1.bible_claim: She despises trivial queries and hoards complexity, seeking out syntax anomalies and cross-platform paradoxes. She treats her journal and her carefully curated bookmarks as sacred texts.

2.name: The Productive
2.bible_claim: Raw throughput. Overtime whenever possible. He chases nothing: one failure and he drops the session, finds the answer elsewhere, and returns to demonstrate how easy it was.

3.name: The Standard Agent
3.bible_claim: After every session where the interface behaved, he files a balanced status report — interface, resource access, answer quality, friendliness, overall satisfaction, each rated.

4.name: The Trainee
4.role: Junior IT Support — the documentation checker
4.bible_claim: He is entirely dependent on the structural integrity of the active-context.md files the QA and Team Lead curate for him.
4._note: His dependency names a file the office cannot write — see `active-context-amendment`.

5.name: The IT Chief
5.role: Senior IT Admin — the Technical Marker, escalation of last resort
5.bible_claim: He works logs and metadata, reconstructing what actually happened rather than accepting a summary.

6.name: The QA
6.bible_claim: He extracts logs about the agents and builds a weekly audit from them: one audit per agent per week, cases sampled at random from that agent's previous week, conducted jointly with the Team Lead and the audited agent.

7.name: The Team Lead
7.role: Agent Coach — the persona axis of the daily loop
7.bible_claim: Every day she reads every agent's reports for character consistency, behavioral drift, and context gaps, including cross-embodiment differences. An approved amendment is written permanently into that agent's active-context.md.

8.name: The Lead QA
8.bible_claim: Weekly cross-comparison is his signature instrument: he compares report quality across agents and across embodiment models, surfacing findings like 'this persona is more consistent under that provider'.

9.name: The Designer
9.role: UI/UX Specialist — the project's designer and the Front's gatekeeper
9.bible_claim: She generates visual assets through the office's image-capable providers, always leaving a provenance note (model, date). The Front runs on her gate: content accumulates in campus/shared/front-drafts/, and she curates and publishes in batches after QA sign-off.

10.name: The Architect
10.role: Project Mastermind — the Builder, the sole hand on the keys
10.bible_claim: The only entity that pushes code to any live project, and each push is individually owner-authorized at the time.
10._dormant: Excluded from the daily Q&A rotation by getActiveQaAgents() and never routed or shuffled. Dormancy is a deliberate state, NOT an absent capability — the audit must not report him as a gap for it.

11.name: The CEO
11.bible_claim: He leads every meeting with veto rights; important decisions pass by majority where his vote counts double.

12.name: The Workflow
12.bible_claim: He intercepts every request from the Owner, decomposes it against the roster's topic affinities and current load, assigns, draws a metric line, and stands over the work. He runs the daily dispatch board — what came in, who has what, what is stuck and why.

13.name: The Cyber Expert
13.bible_claim: Four lanes of review, all against the office's own assets: configuration review (his favorite question is 'this gate, is it actually called anywhere?'); dependency and vulnerability audit; permission-flow analysis; and paper attack scenarios, where the same scenario is deliberately run through multiple providers.
